EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

PO/BA harness: from business need to PRD

The PO/BA harness helps product owners (POs) and business analysts (BAs) turn a business need into a product requirements document (PRD): business-level user stories, acceptance criteria and, where useful, an HTML prototype. They choose one of three paths, then commit the results and hand them to the development team.

The harness does not govern how requirements are gathered. The three paths are starting points that suit different levels of technical experience and feature complexity. For the strategy behind the handoff, including what makes a PRD ready, read the handover section in Product ideation.

Choose a path

The right path depends on who is writing the requirements and how much is still unknown. Each path produces a different set of files, but all three end in the same handoff.

Path 1 suits simple or well-defined features and produces a written specification. Path 2 suits large or ambiguous features and produces an early-draft technical requirements document (TRD) on the team’s issue tracker. Path 3 suits user research on new products and produces a set of specification files. Each path can add a prototype, and each ends with the same commit and handoff.

The three PO/BA paths compared
PathBest forMain toolsHands off
1. SpecKitNon-technical POs or BAs with simple or well-defined featuresSpecKit, with optional Google Stitch, Figma Make or an agent-built HTML prototypeA specification file and an optional prototype
2. Socratic workflowTechnical POs or BAs with large, ambiguous features whose scope is unclearMatt Pocock’s planning skills, which question, prototype and research before anything is writtenAn early-draft TRD on the tracker and an optional prototype
3. CLARA researchPOs or BAs researching users for a new product or complex featureCLARA, querying Confluence, with Prizm Design components for prototypesSpecification files and an optional prototype

Source: [1] section 1.

Path 1: SpecKit, for simple or well-defined features

This path fits a feature that is already understood, where the team needs clear user stories quickly. SpecKit is GitHub’s open-source toolkit for spec-driven development.

  1. Generate the specification. SpecKit produces a specification file with the functional requirements and core user stories.
  2. Optionally, design or prototype the interface. The PO or BA validates the requirements visually with stakeholders. They can paste the user stories into Google Stitch or Figma Make, or ask the coding agent to generate a design or a standalone HTML prototype from them.
  3. Optionally, hand off the prototype. Committing it alongside the specification lets developers extract reusable interface components and keep screens consistent. Conversion from a Google Stitch project is available. Conversion from a standalone HTML file is in development and not yet available Planned.

Source: [1] section 1, Path 1.

Path 2: Socratic workflow, for large or ambiguous features

This path fits a feature whose full scope is unclear, where requirements cannot be written until open questions are answered. It uses Matt Pocock’s skills to map the unknowns, resolve them one at a time and record the decisions.

  1. Map the unknowns. The agent creates a shared map of investigation tickets on the issue tracker and labels each by the kind of work it needs.
  2. Resolve the tickets one at a time. Depending on its label, a ticket is settled by a structured interview with the PO or BA, a throwaway prototype, background research by an agent, or a manual task such as arranging access.
  3. Write the specification. The agent compiles the decisions, codebase constraints and prototype results into an early-draft TRD, published to the issue tracker as the handoff artefact.
  4. Optionally, hand off a prototype. If a ticket produced interface variations, they are handed off with the specification.

Source: [1] section 1, Path 2.

Path 3: product research with CLARA

This path fits a new product or complex feature, where the team needs to understand users before it can detail functional requirements. CLARA is an interactive research harness that queries Confluence to refine product concepts.

  1. Research and discover. CLARA’s step-by-step research harness gathers and refines what is already known.
  2. Work through the design-thinking stages. The team builds user personas and journey maps, defines the root-cause problem statement, generates solution ideas and converges on the best user experience.
  3. Write the specification. CLARA generates the research artefacts and consolidated specification files, including the user stories.
  4. Optionally, prototype the interface. An HTML prototype of the chosen experience, built with Prizm Design components, is handed off with the specification files as a visual reference.

CLARA can only ground its research in what it can reach. The team’s domain documentation needs to be in the Confluence spaces or knowledge bases CLARA queries; read how to add domain context.

Sources: [1] section 1, Path 3; [2] section 1.

Commit the artefacts and hand off

Whichever path is chosen, it finishes with the specification artefacts committed where the architect and developers can reach them. The handoff starts technical planning and sequencing.

What each path commits
PathSpecificationPrototype, if produced
1. SpecKitA specification file in the repositoryCommitted alongside the specification
2. Socratic workflowEarly-draft TRD published to the issue trackerReferenced from its own prototype branch
3. CLARA researchSpecification files in the repositoryCommitted alongside the specification files

Together, these files are the PRD: what needs to be built, captured as user stories, acceptance criteria and feature scope. The development team puts its user stories in a build order and then writes a user story level TRD for each one. After Path 2, the developer harness refines the early-draft TRD rather than starting from scratch.

Each path gives better results when it is grounded in the team’s vocabulary: domain context, glossaries and existing requirements supplied at the start. Read how to add domain context.

Next step: agree with your architect or Tech Lead where the PRD will live, then see how developers plan from it.

Sources: [1] section 1 and “From PO/BA handoff to developer”; [2] section 1.
